quarterly_data.signal: FY2025 RESULTS ABOVE GUIDANCE, 2026 GUIDANCE REAFFIRMED — CEO William J. Fehrman: 'We achieved fourth quarter 2025 operating earnings of $1.19 per share, bringing our full-year 2025 operating earnings to $5.97 per share, which is above the top end of our guidance range.' CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: the result beat 'the high end of our guidance range of $5.75 to $5.95', driven by constructive rate case outcomes, transmission investment and load growth, partly offset by reliability spending, higher depreciation and interest expense. AEP reaffirmed 2026 operating earnings guidance of $6.15 to $6.45 per share (Mihalik: midpoint $6.30, 'I want to underpromise and overdeliver') and its 7% to 9% long-term growth rate for 2026 to 2030 with an expected 9% CAGR. The quarterly dividend was raised in October to $0.95 per share. Fehrman put the 2025 earned ROE on the regulated business at 9.1% (Mihalik cited 'the 9.2' in Q&A), with a path to 'the 9.5' by the end of the five-year plan; S&P FFO to debt was 15.2% at year-end versus a 14% to 15% target (Moody’s just under 14%).
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 2025 operating EPS $1.19; FY2025 $5.97 per share (guidance $5.75 to $5.95); 2026 guidance $6.15 to $6.45 reaffirmed (midpoint $6.30); 7% to 9% long-term growth; earned ROE 9.1%; S&P FFO to debt 15.2%

quarterly_data.signal: DATA-CENTER-LED SALES GROWTH — CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: 'Our total system sales exceeded 200 million megawatt-hours for the first time in AEP history.' Retail sales grew 7.5% in 2025 versus 2024, 'driven by significant commercial and industrial sales growth of nearly 10%, primarily from data centers in Indiana, Texas, and Ohio, as well as industrial sales in Texas'; residential sales grew approximately 3%, mostly I&M and SWEPCO. Because large-load customer agreements include minimum demand charges, 'while total retail sales rose 7.5% in 2025, corresponding revenue was up 8.3%.'
quarterly_data.figure: total system sales over 200 million megawatt-hours; 2025 retail sales +7.5%; commercial and industrial nearly 10%; residential approximately 3%; retail revenue up 8.3%

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LOAD DOUBLES TO 56 GW THROUGH 2030 — CEO William J. Fehrman: 'We now have 56 gigawatts of firm incremental contracted load additions, doubling the 28 gigawatts we reported just last fall. These gigawatts are not speculative as they are all backed by signed customer agreements.' CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: the increase is driven by ERCOT, PJM and SPP. PJM contracted load rose by 4 gigawatts, driven largely by activity in Ohio and reinforced by data center development, with 'about 90% of the incremental PJM load' supported by executed take-or-pay electric service agreements (ESAs); Oklahoma rose by 1 gigawatt, driven primarily by a large aluminum smelting customer. In ERCOT, AEP Texas has signed letters of agreement (LOAs) for 36 gigawatts with large industrial customers, well-capitalized hyperscalers and mega-size data center developers, 'a significant increase of 23 gigawatts since October', all meeting Senate Bill 6 criteria; LOA customers must secure land, pay for interconnection studies and fund all construction costs. Management in Q&A on the load coming in under the ERCOT LOAs: 'more than 50% of that load is now hyperscaler load.' The $72 billion capital plan was built on the prior 28 gigawatt outlook, so capital for the added load is additive and will be addressed with the formal plan update on the third-quarter call.
quarterly_data.figure: 56 gigawatts contracted load by 2030 (from 28 gigawatts); PJM +4 gigawatts (about 90% under take-or-pay ESAs); Oklahoma +1 gigawatt; AEP Texas LOAs 36 gigawatts (+23 gigawatts since October); more than 50% of incoming ERCOT (LOA) load is hyperscaler load

quarterly_data.signal: 180+ GW LOAD QUEUE BEHIND THE 56 GW — CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: 'we still have 180 gigs plus in the queue, in various stages of development', and the queue was not lowered when contracted load was raised. His split: 'roughly about 70 gigs' in ERCOT, 'about 20, 25 gigawatts in AEP Ohio, and then about 30 gigawatts in PSO and another 30 gigawatts in APCo, and then 16 in I&M' (core growth states Texas, Oklahoma, Ohio and Indiana). On Texas: 'Stargate is in Abilene, and that is squarely in our service territory'; the 36 GW of signed LOAs plus almost another 70 GW behind them make '100 gigawatts just in Texas alone', and LNG activity around the Port of Corpus Christi adds 'another 5.1 gigawatts of industrial load'. If any customer walked away, AEP says it 'could backfill that very, very quickly'. CEO William J. Fehrman on ERCOT's new batch study: 'for us, it is positive. We do not see a significant hindrance in this area'; timing of the Texas load depends on SB 6 implementation.
quarterly_data.figure: 180 gigs plus queue: roughly about 70 gigs ERCOT, about 20, 25 gigawatts AEP Ohio, about 30 gigawatts PSO, another 30 gigawatts APCo, 16 in I&M; 100 gigawatts in Texas; 5.1 gigawatts LNG-related industrial load

quarterly_data.signal: $5 BILLION TO $8 BILLION OF UPSIDE TO THE $72 BILLION PLAN — CEO William J. Fehrman calls the $72 billion five-year capital plan (10% rate base CAGR) 'large but conservative'. CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: the plan is based on last fall's 28 GW outlook; since the third-quarter call AEP has identified approximately $5 billion to $8 billion of confirmed or endorsed generation and transmission projects for 2026 through 2030 on top of it, and 'any capital related to the incremental load outlook, which has increased by an additional 28 gigawatts, is additive to our $72 billion plan and is not part of the $5 billion to $8 billion of capital upside'. Breakdown in Q&A: 'about $2.7 billion of transmission projects in SPP, about $1.5 billion in PJM, and about a half billion in MISO', i.e. 'the $4.7 billion, or close to $5 billion, of transmission projects that have either been awarded or kind of assigned to us', plus 'the $2.7 billion associated with the Bloom fuel cells that we announced under the 8-K', for 'roughly $7.4 billion'; only the MISO piece falls outside the five-year window (in service around 2031). Financing and growth-rate implications of the $5 billion to $8 billion are to come on the first-quarter call; the formal capital plan update stays on the third-quarter call.
quarterly_data.figure: $72 billion 2026-2030 plan (10% rate base CAGR); $5 billion to $8 billion upside; transmission $2.7 billion SPP, $1.5 billion PJM, half billion MISO ($4.7 billion); plus $2.7 billion Bloom fuel cells; roughly $7.4 billion identified

quarterly_data.signal: 765 kV FRANCHISE AND EQUIPMENT/CONTRACTOR READINESS — CEO William J. Fehrman: AEP owns and operates 'nearly 90% of the 765 kV infrastructure in the United States', has the largest electric transmission system in the country, and 'was recently recommended for approval or awarded new 765 kV projects in PJM, SPP, and MISO'. AEP leverages its size 'to mitigate supply chain risk'; for the ERCOT build-out it is 'getting well ahead of the equipment supply and the contracting supply', and with its Quanta partnership it is 'the preferred provider of these projects', helped by 'our push to acquire the components that we need well ahead of time'. On interconnection in PJM, SPP and MISO: 'We have the equipment we need. We have the contractors we need.' Once RTO processes clear, execution falls to AEP.
quarterly_data.figure: nearly 90% of the 765 kV infrastructure in the United States

quarterly_data.signal: NEW GENERATION: WYOMING FUEL-CELL PLANT AND SMR SITES — CEO William J. Fehrman: 'last month, we announced plans to purchase $2.65 billion of fuel cells that will be part of a generation facility expected to be located near Cheyenne, Wyoming. The facility includes a 20-year offtake arrangement with a high-quality investment-grade third-party customer.' CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: with a very high-quality counterparty 'signing a 20-year PPA agreement' and no rate case needed, it is 'very similar to a regulated return'. Fehrman frames contracted generation (the Bloom deal and 'perhaps the deployment of batteries') as a way to bring data centers online significantly faster where grid connection could be a couple of years out: 'It is clearly a proven technology that can be deployed relatively quickly.' AEP is also participating in the early site permit process for two potential small modular reactor (SMR) locations, in Indiana and Virginia, and will move forward only 'with the appropriate returns and risk mitigating structures'. On generation adequacy: 'For our load within our own VIUs, we believe we have sufficient resources to meet our current growth projections.'
quarterly_data.figure: $2.65 billion of fuel cells (Wyoming); 20-year offtake; two potential SMR locations (Indiana, Virginia)

quarterly_data.signal: LARGE-LOAD TARIFFS — CEO William J. Fehrman: AEP secured commission approvals two years ago for data center tariffs in Ohio and large load tariff modifications in Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia, and 'now have pending tariff filings in Michigan, Oklahoma, Texas, and Virginia', designed so existing customers do not bear the cost of grid improvements needed for data-center demand. Legislation reducing regulatory lag was approved in Ohio, Oklahoma and Texas; base rate cases in Arkansas, Kentucky and Ohio were approved or settled, with new cases filed in Oklahoma and Texas. CFO Trevor Ian Mihalik: the ESAs have a take-or-pay component and the large load tariffs 'lock those counterparties in place'.
quarterly_data.figure: approved: Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia; pending: Michigan, Oklahoma, Texas, Virginia
